title: The lamp
hook: Agni hides; why the lamp is lit first and greeted
carry: the lamp's light is greeted as god

segments.voice: Yesterday, five objects on a shelf, and Dhanna's ordinary rock. Your line was the murti is an honored guest. Today, the second object.

The power goes out at night. The fridge stops humming. Everyone goes quiet. Somebody fumbles in a drawer, finds a candle, strikes a match. And the whole room changes. Faces come back. People talk more softly, as if the little flame were listening. Many Hindu homes light a flame on purpose, every evening, even when the power is fine. It's the second object on the shelf, and it comes with one of the oldest stories in Hinduism.
screen: `THE POWER GOES OUT.` → `ONE MATCH, AND THE ROOM CHANGES.` → `ONE OF HINDUISM'S OLDEST STORIES.`

segments.voice: In the oldest hymns, the Rig Veda, fire is a god: Agni, the one who carries every offering up to the gods. And one hymn tells how Agni ran away. He was afraid of the work; the fires before him, he says, had worn out in that service. So he hid, deep in the waters and the plants, and the offerings had no one to carry them. The gods went looking, found him, and coaxed him: come back. They promised him a share of the offerings and a life that wouldn't age. And Agni came out and took his place again, between the people and the gods. That's the flame in a Hindu home. The Sanskrit word for the lamp is deepa, from a root meaning to shine. Often it's a small clay diya with a cotton wick in ghee or oil, lit at dawn and at dusk, and often lit as puja begins. Many families greet it with a short verse beginning shubham karoti kalyanam, honoring the lamp's light for bringing what is good and pushing away what harms. Many go on: deepa jyoti parabrahma, the lamp's light is the supreme Brahman. That's the teaching. The flame isn't only a sign that God is near. Many Hindus greet the light itself as God, the one reality shining in everything, small enough to sit in a clay bowl. So it's lit first, and bowed to. And people point out one more thing: when one lamp lights another, it loses nothing. That's why, back on day five, arti was light passed hand to hand.
screen: `AGNI HIDES IN THE WATERS.` · `THE GODS COAX HIM BACK.` · `DEEPA — FROM A ROOT: TO SHINE.` · `DEEPA JYOTI PARABRAHMA.` · then, large: `THE LAMP'S LIGHT IS GREETED AS GOD.`

segments.voice: If it's safe, light a candle or a lamp somewhere steady, away from anything that can catch; if not, picture one. Let your eyes rest on the flame softly, without staring hard, and notice how it moves with your breath, the bright middle, the blue at the base. Then close your eyes for a moment, see if the shape of it stays, and open them: one flame, that's all.
Deepa. The lamp: a small flame, from a root meaning to shine, lit at the edges of the day and greeted as God.
Your line: the lamp's light is greeted as God. One flame, and it loses nothing when it's shared. Until tomorrow.
